messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan is a 36-year-old South Asian man who was divorced several years ago. As an accountant, he works long hours at a busy firm in downtown Chicago. Rohan has always been sensitive to the environment around him due to his childhood experiences of witnessing domestic violence between his parents. The traumatic event still lingers vividly in his mind. One evening, when Rohan was about 10 years old, he heard violent shouting and crashing from another room. When he cautiously approached, he saw his mother being violently assaulted by his father. The sound of shattering glass, the terrified look on his mother’s face, and the feeling of utter helplessness are memories that still bring back the same terror Rohan felt at the time. These vivid memories have shaped Rohan's current life in profound ways. Whenever he hears a sudden loud noise or sees an argument between two people, his body immediately tenses up and goes on high alert. He often finds himself scanning his surroundings for any signs of danger, even when he is in safe environments like his office or at home. Rohan had come to believe that the people responsible for such violence have faced no consequences, which has reinforced a sense of helplessness. This belief exacerbates his constant state of hypervigilance and physical reactivity. When something in his surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, he experiences intense panic and anxiety. For example, the sound of shattering glass at work triggers him to relive that terrifying moment from his childhood. The terror on recall has also made Rohan feel like a miserable person who used to be much happier before these traumatic memories began to dominate his life. The experience has deeply affected his ability to trust others and enjoy daily activities without fear. This pervasive sense of helplessness makes it even harder for him to cope with the intrusive memories that constantly resurface. Over time, Rohan’s negative appraisals have intensified his symptoms. He is certain that he can't stop bad things from happening to him, which contributes to his heightened physical reactions and hypervigilance. This constant state of fear has led to a cycle where his threat perception feeds into the intensity and frequency of his traumatic memories. For instance, at work, if Rohan hears colleagues arguing over details in financial reports, it can trigger an immediate sense of dread and anxiety, leading him to avoid eye contact or any interaction that might remind him of the violence he witnessed as a child. This avoidance has strained some professional relationships and made social interactions stressful for him. The combination of these symptoms finally brought Rohan to seek help when he realized his work performance was declining due to frequent absences and difficulty concentrating. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again, but at the same time, he hopes that with therapy, he can regain some control over his life and find a way to manage his overwhelming memories and fears.
